phases.title: Clean and document
phases.why: Know exactly what you have before changing anything.

tasks.t: Photograph both sides of the board in high resolution
tasks.n: Your before picture. You'll reference these constantly while tracing.

tasks.t: Clean the corrosion with 99% isopropyl alcohol and a soft brush
tasks.n: Gentle first. Heat and flux only on joints that still look bad after cleaning.

tasks.t: Inspect under magnification and log every IC, the regulator, and the crystal markings
tasks.n: Write down U1–U5 part numbers and the frequency printed on Y1.

tasks.t: Sketch the board's zones: power input, regulator, relays/optocouplers, safety input, display, keypad
tasks.n: The safety cutoff circuit is probably where the optocouplers live. Worth understanding even if you won't use it.

phases.title: Bring up power
phases.why: Get a clean, safe 5V onto the chip's rail.

tasks.t: Find VDD (pin 20) and VSS (pins 8 and 19) and follow them to the board's power rail
Identify the regulator and where the ribbon cable used to bring power in
Feed 5V from a USB breakout into the rail after the regulator
tasks.n: Use a current-limited bench supply at school for the first power-up if one is available (about 100 mA limit).

tasks.t: Measure 5V at pin 20 and note the board's current draw

phases.title: Map the board
phases.why: The pin map is the foundation for all your code. This is where Fusion earns its keep.

tasks.t: Confirm header E3 is the programming header
tasks.n: Continuity to MCLR (1), VDD (20), VSS (8/19), PGC (27), PGD (28).

tasks.t: Trace each display segment and digit-select line to its PIC pin
tasks.n: Note whether the display is common anode or common cathode, and whether transistors drive the digits.

tasks.t: Trace LEDs DS3–DS7 and the keypad header E2 to their PIC pins
Check whether RC3/RC4 (I²C pins) are free or already wired to something
tasks.n: That decides where the RTC connects.

tasks.t: Build a pin map table: PIC pin → net → what it drives

phases.title: Set up the toolchain
phases.why: Get the programmer and software ready before touching the chip.

tasks.t: Check MPLAB X's supported-device list for PIC16F73 with the programmer you plan to buy
tasks.n: PICkit 4 or 5 is the safer choice than a PICkit 3 for current MPLAB X.

tasks.t: Get a PICkit and header pins or jumper wires
Install MPLAB X IDE and the XC8 compiler
Read the datasheet sections on I/O ports, Timer0/Timer1, and configuration bits

phases.title: First contact
phases.why: Talk to the chip without breaking anything you can't undo.

tasks.t: Connect the PICkit and read the device ID
tasks.n: Power the board yourself rather than from the PICkit.

tasks.t: Read and save the factory firmware as a .hex file before any erase
tasks.n: If it isn't code-protected, keep it. Disassembling it is a bonus project.

tasks.t: Blink one LED in assembly
tasks.n: About 20 instructions. Code by Petzold, made real.

tasks.t: Blink the same LED in C with XC8

phases.title: Drive the display
phases.why: Go from one segment to a full counting display.

tasks.t: Light a single segment
Show any digit 0–9 on one position using a lookup table
Multiplex all three digits from a timer interrupt
Run a test counter from 000 to 999

phases.title: Keep time and remember it
phases.why: Make it a real day counter that survives power loss.

tasks.t: Build a 1-second timebase with Timer1 and measure its drift against your phone over 24 hours
Wire a DS3231 RTC module with coin cell to the I²C pins
tasks.n: The common ZS-042 module also has a small EEPROM. Store the start date there.

tasks.t: Compute days = today's date − start date and show it on the display
Add a keypad button to reset the start date
Pull the power, wait, restore it, and confirm the count is correct

phases.title: Enclosure
phases.why: Make it a finished object for your desk.

tasks.t: Measure the board, mounting holes, display window, and connectors with calipers
Model the enclosure in Tinkercad with your CSA teacher
Print, test-fit, and revise

phases.title: Version 2 (later)
phases.why: Only after v1 works. Options to explore, not commitments.

tasks.t: Look into a PIC16F886 as a replacement chip
tasks.n: Same 28-pin family, adds data EEPROM and an internal oscillator. Confirm the pinout against both datasheets first.

tasks.t: Add a Pico W that gets exact time over Wi-Fi and sends it to the PIC over UART
tasks.n: Needs a level shifter: the Pico is 3.3V, the PIC is 5V.

tasks.t: Design a single custom PCB in KiCad or Fusion with a fresh chip and the RTC on board
Write up the build with code, the pin map, and photos
